store.0: I'm a Computer Science major in my fourth year. My schedule this semester is quite packed, but it's exciting to be taking higher-level courses that I've been looking forward to. It's surreal to think about how far I've come since my freshman year, when I was learning about basic data structures. Now, I'm diving into complex algorithmic concepts, advanced system design, and even exploring the basics of quantum computing. It's amazing how quickly time has passed.

store.21: I'm a fourth-year computer science major, and my schedule can get really hectic with classes and projects. My hobbies are what keep me sane, to be honest. It's funny - as intense as coding can be, I actually love everything about it. I find that my outside interests help me come back to programming with a fresh perspective. I believe it's essential to take a break and not be stuck behind my laptop 24/7, even if I do enjoy tinkering with code.
store.22: Sailing is probably the first thing that comes to mind when people ask me about my hobbies. It's unique among my friends, and it's something I've been passionate about since I was younger. Growing up, my dad would take me out on these tiny sailboats near the marina. The moment I felt the rush of wind against the sails, I was hooked. Now in college, I try to keep up with sailing whenever I go back home for breaks. There's a local sailing club that rents out boats at a student-friendly rate, so I'll sign up for a day, invite a friend if they're interested, and spend hours on the water. I love the sense of freedom it gives me. Everything else – looming deadlines, bug fixes in code, group project drama – fades into the background. Out on the water, the conditions are unpredictable, and you have to stay focused. It's like solving a puzzle on a grand scale, which I think is why it appeals to my problem-solving side.
store.23: I'm also really passionate about going to the gym regularly. In high school, I was the scrawny kid who spent most of my time hunched over a computer. However, once I got to college, I realized I needed to find a way to offset the sedentary lifestyle that came with studying. I started with a basic lifting routine in my freshman year, thanks to a friend from my dorm who taught me the fundamentals of proper form for squats and deadlifts, as well as how to program workouts. Now, I try to hit the gym around four times a week. It's not about becoming a bodybuilder; I just love seeing the incremental improvements in my strength and energy levels. If I can lift a bit more weight this month than last, or if I have a bit more energy in my daily life, I consider that a win. Additionally, going to the gym is a great stress-reliever after marathon coding sessions. The mental clarity I get after a good workout is truly amazing. It makes me more productive and helps me sleep better, especially on those nights when I'm up late finishing an assignment.
store.24: Gaming is another hobby that's closely related to my interest in technology. I'm a fan of both PC and console games, but I spend more time on PC since it's my go-to platform as a CS major. Lately, I've been really into co-op survival games where you gather resources, build shelters, and fend off creatures. I enjoy the problem-solving aspect of these games, as it's a bit more relaxed compared to debugging code. Occasionally, I also jump into fast-paced shooters, especially when my classmates are online and we team up. It's a social activity and a mental challenge all rolled into one. While some might view gaming as a waste of time, I believe it can be strategic and collaborative, and it's a great way to stay connected with friends. I've also dabbled in game development using Unity and Unreal Engine for fun. I'd love to explore this further if I have the time, as bridging the gap between playing games and creating them is really exciting.
store.25: Reading has been a lifelong passion of mine, thanks to my mom's love for literature. She used to hand me fantasy and sci-fi novels when I was a kid, and I'd get lost in other worlds for hours. Even with a busy schedule now, I try to squeeze in some reading before bed or on weekends. Lately, I've been fascinated by sci-fi novels that explore artificial intelligence. It's partly driven by my academic interests, as I enjoy imagining future technology and how it might blur the boundaries between humans and machines. My current favorite AI-themed sci-fi book is 'The Infinity Courts' by Akemi Dawn Bowman. These books not only provide relaxation but also help me consider the ethical and social implications of the work I'll be doing after graduation. In a way, reading is both a hobby and a means of exploring philosophical questions related to my field of study.
store.26: I know it might seem like juggling all these hobbies would be chaotic, but I've found that scheduling them helps me maintain a healthy balance. I treat my hobbies just like I would my study time – I plan them out. For example, every Sunday, I look at my week ahead and check the weather to see if it's suitable for a gym session in the afternoon or a trip to the local lake to rent a dinghy. If the weather isn't cooperating, I'll plan an indoor day with friends, either playing co-op games or working out in my apartment's fitness center. As for reading, it's the easiest to fit in – I aim for 30 minutes before bedtime, which is a great way to unwind after a long day. By scheduling my hobbies, I'm able to make time for everything that brings me joy and fulfillment.
store.27: I also enjoy combining my hobbies. For example, I've had a day where I spent the morning sailing at the lake, then grabbed lunch, and ended the day playing video games with friends. It was fascinating to see how the experience on the water was similar to coordinating movement in an online co-op. In both cases, everyone has a specific role – whether it's manning the sails or leading the in-game strategy. I love how each hobby, in its own way, demands teamwork, attention to detail, and problem-solving. It's great to see how different activities can complement each other and enhance my overall experience.
store.28: Of course, there are days when it can get overwhelming. Between lectures, labs, homework, research group meetings, and my part-time tutoring gig, a significant portion of my day is consumed by academic responsibilities. However, I believe that when you're truly passionate about your hobbies, you'll find ways to incorporate them into your schedule, even if it's just in small increments. For example, I might not have hours to read, but I can fit in one chapter. I might not be able to sail every weekend, but once a month works. And with gaming, even 30 minutes can be enough for a quick match. It's all about finding those small pockets of time and making the most of them.
store.29: The best part about my hobbies is that they give me something to talk about outside of coding. I love discussing data structures and algorithms, but it's great to have other interests that showcase a different side of me. My hobby menu ranges from the calming world of reading to the thrilling experience of sailing, from the discipline of weightlifting to the adrenaline rush of co-op games. Having these diverse interests makes life more exciting and engaging. I'm glad I could share my passion with you – thanks for listening!
store.30: I've been involved in undergraduate research since the end of my sophomore year, and it's been one of the most eye-opening parts of my college experience. It's given me a glimpse into how knowledge is created in the tech world, and it's really cool to be a part of that. When I was a freshman, I didn't see myself going down the research route. I was into coding projects and hackathons, but I didn't think of research as something that was 'my thing.' However, one of my professors, who taught an introductory data science class, noticed that I had a knack for bridging technical coding with user experience. She told me about an opening for a research assistant in a lab focused on data visualization for big scientific datasets. I was initially hesitant because research seemed intimidating. However, I decided to take the leap, and it turned out to be a great decision.
store.31: The lab I'm in is an interdisciplinary space where computer scientists partner with scientists from various backgrounds, such as astronomy, environmental science, and neuroscience, to make massive amounts of data more comprehensible. In classes, you might work with small data sets or a 1GB dataset for a machine learning project. However, in our lab, we deal with datasets that are tens of terabytes in size. Visualizing such large datasets so that domain experts(like astrophysicists) can quickly extract insights is a significant challenge. One of my main tasks is to work on front-end prototypes that present slices of data in dynamic, interactive dashboards. This involves using advanced JavaScript frameworks, custom visualizations with D3.js, and specialized libraries for volumetric rendering if we're dealing with 3D data.
store.32: The first research project I really got into was about visualizing oceanic temperature changes over time for a climate study group. They had these daily temperature readings from buoys all around the Pacific. The raw data was enormous, consisting of tons of files scattered across different servers, each representing a single day's worth of readings at tiny intervals. Our job was to aggregate and present them in a coherent way that could show patterns over months or even years. I dove in headfirst, writing scripts to clean and unify the data, building a pipeline that could handle near real-time updates, and then designing interfaces that let researchers zoom into a particular region or timeframe. Eventually, I co-authored my first paper on this system. I have to admit, I freaked out a bit when I saw my name in an official publication—it felt so surreal. It's probably one of my proudest moments in college.
store.33: These days, my research has shifted to a slightly different area, still under the umbrella of data visualization. I'm currently working on immersive analytics platforms. We're exploring how VR or AR technologies can help scientists gain a more intuitive understanding of complex data. Think about it: looking at raw numerical data in a spreadsheet is one thing, and 2D visuals like graphs are another step up. However, being able to walk around a 3D representation of data in a virtual environment, touch it, rotate it, and highlight subsets could be a game-changer for certain fields. It's a significant leap from just coding up websites. There's a lot of experimentation involved, such as plugging in VR headsets, integrating with engines like Unity or Unreal, and figuring out how to efficiently stream data into a 3D environment. It's all very cutting-edge, which makes it exciting. Every day, you're forging your own path because there isn't a large, established best-practice library for VR data visualization yet.
store.34: The reality of research life is quite different from what many people imagine. It's not just about coding away on a mysterious project in a quiet corner. In fact, a significant part of research involves reading. Academic papers seem to never end, and when I'm trying to solve a bug with rendering volumetric data in VR, there's a good chance someone has attempted something similar and written about it in a conference proceeding or workshop. I need to comb through those papers to find relevant information. It can be overwhelming at times, but over time, you learn how to skim effectively by looking at the abstract, introduction, and conclusion to determine if a paper is relevant before diving into the details. Occasionally, when I discover something interesting, I'll share it with the rest of the lab, and we'll discuss how we can incorporate that technique into our own workflow.
store.35: I also get to interact with a bunch of graduate students, both master's and PhD students. It can be intimidating at first because they're so deeply immersed in their niche fields, but it's also inspiring. There's this one PhD student in our lab who's been developing a machine learning algorithm for on-the-fly compression of large datasets. He's trying to integrate it with our VR platform. The idea is that when looking at a huge climate dataset, you don't need to have every single point fully loaded at once in VR—a compressed representation might be enough until you zoom in. It's a wild concept, but it's super practical for real-time performance. Working alongside him means I get to see how advanced theoretical concepts are actually applied. Some of our best brainstorming sessions happen spontaneously, like in the lab break room, sipping coffee and hashing out how we can offload some processing to the GPU.
store.36: We've also had the opportunity to present our research at smaller symposiums around campus through poster presentations. It was a great experience. We had to distill our complex research into easy-to-understand visuals and talking points. The first time I presented, I was nervous, but it turned out to be a friendly dialogue. People are genuinely interested in what you're doing. There were even a few folks from local startups who attended, and they shared interesting perspectives on how VR for data visualization could benefit commercial industries, such as marketing analytics or architecture. It opened my eyes to how research can transition from academia to real-world applications.
store.37: As for publications, I've been fortunate enough to be a co-author on two workshop papers and I'm currently working on a larger conference submission. The conference we're targeting is the IEEE Visualization Conference(IEEE VIS), which is a significant event in our field. We're focusing on a user study that compares traditional 2D dashboards with an interactive VR environment. Our hypothesis is that VR immersion helps researchers spot anomalies or trends faster than they would with a plain old 2D chart. To test this, we conducted a small user trial with 15 participants, recording their times and asking them to fill out a UX questionnaire. Now we're analyzing the data to determine if there's a statistically significant difference. Writing the paper is a collaborative effort: I'm handling the sections on system architecture and prototype design, while someone else is writing about the user study methodology. Our principal investigator is weaving it all together into a cohesive narrative. It's a balancing act, especially with my senior coursework and capstone project to manage.
store.38: Sometimes I get asked if I plan on going to grad school myself. Right now, I'm leaning towards working in the industry for a couple of years, hopefully at a tech company that values R&D or advanced solution building, before deciding if I want to pursue a master's or PhD. The idea of contributing to cutting-edge knowledge is really tempting, especially in areas like data visualization or machine learning. However, I also want to see how these concepts get applied in real product development. One of my mentors in the lab said that sometimes stepping into industry can give you a better perspective on what problems are truly relevant, so that if you do come back for a PhD, you'll have a more practical approach.
store.39: It's not all sunshine and rainbows, though. Research can be frustrating. You might spend weeks on an approach that doesn't pan out, or you might discover that your entire idea has already been done—and improved upon—by a group in Europe or somewhere else. That can be a tough pill to swallow. However, the key is to adapt. We'll read that existing paper, incorporate their findings, think of a new angle or a new application, and push the boundary. That's the essence of research. You're never truly starting from scratch; you're building on this giant foundation of what others have done. The sense of collaboration—both within our lab and among the global research community—is something I find really special.
store.40: One story that really stands out was when one of our massive servers crashed a few months ago. We had vital data stored there, some of which wasn't fully backed up(I know, rookie mistake, but we learned from it). I remember the scramble that night: a frantic email chain, Zoom calls with the lab manager, everyone trying to see if we could recover the data. We managed to restore most of it, but that crisis hammered home the importance of data backups. After that fiasco, we set up a better backup system and implemented some checks to ensure we never again rely on a single point of failure. It was stressful, but also kind of a bonding experience for the whole lab.
store.41: Another big plus of research is that it connects me with professors on a more personal level than just being a face in the lecture hall. My PI is super approachable, and if I have a question about the direction of my career or something I'm struggling with in class, I know I can pop into her office and chat. She's been recommending me for different scholarships, events, and networking opportunities. I even got to attend a virtual workshop on immersive analytics that was filled with academic experts from all around the world. Witnessing them debate technical details, propose new frameworks, and even gently tease each other over rival theories was fascinating. It was like I was witnessing the frontier of CS knowledge in real time.
store.42: That's basically my journey in the research world so far. It's a lot of work, often more chaotic than you'd expect, but also super rewarding. I love the feeling that what I do in the lab might end up shaping the way scientists understand their data five or ten years down the line. Maybe one day the VR and immersive stuff we're trying to pioneer will become standard tools, and I'll be able to look back and say, 'Hey, I was part of that from the beginning.' It's that sense of contributing to something bigger that really keeps me motivated. Whether or not I go to grad school soon, I know this experience has changed how I think about computer science, about innovation, and even about teamwork. I couldn't imagine my undergrad years without it—it's definitely enriched my whole perspective on what it means to be a computer scientist.
